item.title: Students lose shared rooms to studios as landlords sell
item.description:
Students lose shared rooms to studios as landlords sell

August 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Small private landlords are selling off cheap, shared housing that students depend on, new figures from the land registry Kadaster show.

Across the Dutch cities with a university, these private landlords cut the number of homes they rent out by 19% on average over three years, according to NRC, which reported the figures.

Bigger property companies bought and built enough to keep the total number of rental homes almost steady, and student cities are attractive to investors, but these tend to be smaller studios rather than shared houses.

For a student hunting a room, that means there are likely fewer affordable shared rooms and more competition.

Hardest on internationals
International students are hardest hit by this, as they cannot join the years-long waiting lists for social housing, which the Kadaster figures don’t include, and often have to rent from abroad without seeing the room first.

That leaves them relying on the private market, which is shrinking, and more exposed to scams and overcharging.

It is not the same everywhere though – the number of rental homes actually rose in Amsterdam, Leiden and Eindhoven, while The Hague and Utrecht saw the steepest falls.

The national shortage stood at 21,500 rooms last year, and more students are giving up the search and staying with their parents, according to student housing centre Kences, which has linked the sell-off to lost rooms. Its next report is due on September 3.

Housing minister Elanor Boekholt-O’Sullivan this week asked councils to be more flexible about shared student houses, after 10 students in Groningen faced eviction because their council would not treat them as one household.

item.title: Amsterdam mayor wants to scrap fines for sleeping outdoors
item.description:
Amsterdam mayor wants to scrap fines for sleeping outdoors

August 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Amsterdam mayor Femke Halsema wants to decriminalise sleeping outdoors, despite objections from residents of the Plantage neighbourhood in the east of the city.

Residents have launched a petition to prevent that from happening, according to AT5. Sleeping on the street or in parks is technically a fineable offence, although in practice no one has been fined over the past year. The mayor now wants it to become official policy.

Plantage resident Dennis de Vreede, who supports the petition, said he fears scrapping criminal liability will lead to more people sleeping outdoors, more nuisance and less possibilities for official action – despite acknowledging that fines are pointless.

“These people cannot afford it and might end up in even more debt trouble,” he told AT5. “But the entire legal framework collapses, meaning the police can no longer take action at all.”

“Shameful” fines

Halsema called fining sleeping homeless people “shameful” in 2021 and has said the measure doesn’t even work. “The intention is that the fine will bring about a change in behaviour,” she wrote, but she questioned whether it actually reduces nuisance.

From 2021 to 2024, fines were only issued for nuisance resulting from sleeping outdoors. Some 1,800 fines were handed out in that period.

But Bianca Koster of the Rainbow Group agrees that fining has little effect. “It helps to address the visibility, but not the core of the problem,” she said.

What needs to be addressed, she said, is why people end up on the streets. She called for more shelters, more care and more housing.

“I understand that when it gets visibly worse, people think we have to do something,” she said. “But punishing people is not the way.”

item.title: Heavy thunderstorms expected this evening
item.description:
Heavy thunderstorms expected this evening

August 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Following Thursday’s oppressive daytime humidity and heat – with temperatures ranging between 25° and 30° – the night will see rain and thunderstorms in the south of the country moving north, reports the KNMI weather service.

“During the showers, wind gusts of up to 60 km/h are possible,” said the weather service, and “there is a chance of hail up to 2 cm and heavy rain may fall in a short time”.

While no official warnings have currently been issued, KNMI said there’s a possibility of wind gusts, downed trees and local flooding.

The weather service has just launched a thunderstorm notification app to alert people of local storms happening within 15 minutes of where they are. Currently operating as a beta test through August 31 in the KNMI app, you can download it here and provide feedback later.

item.title: New agreement secures healthcare for 20,000 refugee children
item.description:
New agreement secures healthcare for 20,000 refugee children

August 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The national refugee settlement agency COA has secured a three-year contract with public health body GGD to ensure that the nearly 20,000 children living in Dutch asylum centres will continue to receive uninterrupted healthcare.

The current contract was due to expire in October while another with a separate health body wouldn’t come into effect until June 2027, leaving a potential 8-month gap that led six children’s ombudsmen to brand “a serious violation of children’s rights”.

“The decision to award GGD GHOR Nederland a new three-year contract brings stability and clarity,” said André Rouvoet, chairman of GGD GHOR Nederland.

“Accessible youth healthcare is of great importance for asylum-seeking children. With this period, we can continue to do what is necessary: ​​provide accessible, expert, and preventive care.”

Children’s rights organizations were concerned that a gap in care could lead to lower levels of vaccination and a decrease in flagging health and mental health issues.

While regular medical and emergency care are available to refugees, without the new funding, preventative care – which also includes consultations, growth checks and developmental assessments – could have fallen through the cracks.

item.title: New funding for long Covid research centre raised
item.description:
New funding for long Covid research centre raised

August 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Long COVID Foundation (SLC) has launched a National Research & Innovation Center to investigate long covid in the Netherlands as government money has dried up.

With some €40 million the government provided for research having been spent and no new budget yet allocated, the foundation awarded €500,000 to seven researchers to keep their research going and to “translate scientific discoveries more quickly into diagnostics and targeted treatments for adults and children.”

“SLC wants to prevent years of investment, knowledge and research power from being lost.”

The money is being given to researchers from the hospitals Amsterdam UMC, the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, UMC Utrecht and Erasmus MC. The foundation’s goal is that the centre, operating as an independent foundation and an open national research network, will be a central hub for stimulating and linking research under one national program.

Still no treatment

Calling long covid “one of the great unresolved medical challenges of our time”, the foundation estimates 400,000 people have been affected by it – 100,000 of them seriously. “Yet there are no proven healing treatment, effective diagnostics and targeted therapies yet.”

Long covid sufferers struggle with fatigue, brain fog, loss of concentration, and memory and immune system problems that have severely limited their ability to work and lead normal lives.

Targeted treatments

The foundation says it’s becoming increasingly clear that long covid suffers can be distinguished by groups. “An important task for the centre will be to better distinguish these groups and to investigate which treatments can work in which patients.”

The foundation is also looking into other the post-acute infection syndromes, such as ME/CFS, a chronic illness characterised by an inability to function.

In the future, says SLC, “long-term public and private financing is also needed”.

“The stronger and more structural the research is organized, the more likely it is that scientific discoveries will lead to the diagnostics and targeted treatments that patients have been waiting for so long.”

item.title: Summer 2026 was Netherlands’ hottest ever recorded
item.description:
Summer 2026 was Netherlands’ hottest ever recorded

August 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The summer of 2026 was the warmest in the Netherlands since national records began in 1901, figures from the KNMI weather service show.

The average temperature at the KNMI’s benchmark station in De Bilt reached 19.3° over the three summer months, beating the previous record (set in 2018) of 18.9° by nearly half a degree. With August almost over, the record is already beyond reach, broadcaster NOS reported.

In June the KNMI issued its first-ever code red warning for extreme heat, a level not triggered even during the record temperatures of 2019. The country then went through multiple heatwaves, and the public health institute RIVM has linked at least 900 excess deaths to the June spell alone.

The nights were also extremely hot. In Maastricht, the temperature stayed above 22° for three nights running for the first time, which has never been recorded anywhere in the Netherlands before, even over two nights.

Peter Siegmund, a climate expert at the KNMI, told NOS that a summer this warm can now be expected roughly once every five years in the current climate – an interval he expects to shorten as warming continues.

Under the KNMI’s highest climate scenario, he said, a summer of this kind would be an average one by around 2050.

item.title: US tech firm drops takeover bid for DigiD operator Solvinity
item.description:
US tech firm drops takeover bid for DigiD operator Solvinity

August 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The American IT services company Kyndryl has abandoned its attempt to buy Solvinity, the Amsterdam-based firm that runs the hosting platform behind DigiD, ending a takeover the Dutch government blocked in May on national security grounds.

A company spokesperson told the NRC that Kyndryl no longer wants to acquire Solvinity. The company’s latest quarterly report to US regulators also noted that the €100 million deal had been prohibited and that Solvinity’s owners were weighing their response.

DigiD is the login that millions of people in the Netherlands use to file tax returns and reach health insurers, pension funds and local councils. Solvinity runs the platform it sits on, along with the Berichtenbox message service in the MijnOverheid portal, and also supplies the justice ministry.

Security concerns
The takeover, announced last November, alarmed MPs and security experts because it would have brought the data behind DigiD within reach of the US Cloud Act, which can compel American-owned companies to hand over information even when it is held on servers in Europe.”

Junior digital economy minister Willemijn Aerdts blocked the sale in late May “to protect the public interest”, acting on advice from the BTI, the agency that vets foreign investments for security risks.

What happens next
Solvinity, owned by the British private equity firm Vitruvian Partners, is appealing. A Rotterdam judge refused to suspend the ban in July but told Aerdts to weigh a lighter measure than an outright ban.

Aerdts is due to rule on the company’s objection by the end of September. Solvinity and its owners are “exploring remedies, including contesting the government’s decision”, according to Kyndryl’s filing, and may also pursue a claim against Kyndryl.

The current DigiD contract runs until August 2028. The government has said the successor contract will be tendered under defence and security procurement rules that let it exclude bidders from countries whose laws could force access to Dutch data – meaning the platform’s next operator will have to be European.

item.title: Murder rate falls to record low but femicide rate unchanged
item.description:
Murder rate falls to record low but femicide rate unchanged

August 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The share of women killed by a partner in the Netherlands has not shifted in 15 years, even as the country’s overall murder toll fell to its lowest level since records began, figures from the national statistics office CBS showed on Thursday.

A total of 103 people were killed by murder or manslaughter in 2025, 17 fewer than a year earlier. The fall was driven by a drop in male victims, which reached a 30-year low.

But between 2021 and 2025, just over half of all women killed died at the hands of a current or former partner – rising to 63% among those aged 20 to 60.

Killed by a partner
Just over half of all female victims between 2021 and 2025 were killed by a current or former partner, a proportion that has not changed for 15 years. Among women aged 20 to 60, it rose to 63%.

Police identified a suspect in 96% of cases involving women. A further 18% were killed by another relative, 16% by an acquaintance and 9% by a stranger.

The picture for men was different. A suspect was identified in 86% of cases; nearly a third of male victims were killed by an acquaintance, and 11% died in what CBS called a settling of scores in the criminal underworld.

Children and cities
The statistics office also recorded the deaths of 24 children under the age of 10 over the five-year period. In 20 of those cases, the suspected killer was the child’s own mother or father.

Rotterdam saw the most victims between 2021 and 2025, with 65, followed by Amsterdam with 62. There were 36 in The Hague and 12 in Utrecht. A quarter of all victims were killed in the four largest cities.

CBS noted that it cannot separate murder from manslaughter, or suspects from convicted perpetrators, because many of the cases had not come to trial when the court files were compiled.

Political response
The constant rate of partner killings has fuelled growing political concern about femicide. In June, the cabinet moved to make coercive control a criminal offence for the first time, calling controlling behaviour a frequent precursor to such killings.

A study for the justice ministry in May found that Dutch courts almost never use the word “femicide” in their verdicts, even in cases that fit international definitions.

If you have experienced or are experiencing domestic or sexual violence, Veilig Thuis (Safe at Home) offers confidential advice 24 hours a day on 0800 2000 or at veiligthuis.nl. In an emergency, call 112.

item.title: Dutch chip industry turnover doubles to €46bn in six years
item.description:
Dutch chip industry turnover doubles to €46bn in six years

August 27, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch semiconductor industry has more than doubled in six years, with turnover reaching €46 billion in 2025, according to the first detailed measurement of the sector by the national statistics office CBS.

The industry’s national turnover stood at €21 billion in 2019, CBS said, growing by an average of 14% a year since. Employment nearly doubled over the same period, from 23,000 people to more than 43,000.

The figures are provisional estimates from a new method CBS is still developing, which combines its own data with government figures. They cover more than 300 companies – not only chipmakers and the machine builders that supply them, but firms providing parts and services to the sector.

Not just ASML
ASML, the Veldhoven-based maker of the world’s most advanced chip machines, is also the country’s most valuable listed company. It reported record worldwide sales of €32.7 billion in 2025 and employs around 20,000 people in the Netherlands.

Newer companies are also adding to the total, with companies entering the sector since 2019 accounting for about €400 million in growth, CBS said. Firms such as chip metrology company Nearfield Instruments, which raised $380 million this year, are among those trying to build positions alongside ASML.

Chips and AI
The sector’s growth comes with the boom in AI, globalisation and security, which CBS is now studying more closely. “AI is highly dependent on chips. The semiconductor industry is therefore the technical engine beneath all the developments we are seeing in the field of AI,” said Marjolijn Jaarsma, CBS’s international trade spokesperson.

Dennis Cremers, the project lead behind the research, said the industry was one of the most globalised in the world. “Take the newest GPU and AI chips: they are designed in the United States and manufactured in East Asia using, among other things, Dutch machines,” he said.

“Ultimately they end up in enormous datacentres where the newest AI models are trained. The Netherlands has a unique role in this, particularly in machine-building.”

item.title: MPs want to scrap far-right TV show over “Hitler was right” item
item.description:
MPs want to scrap far-right TV show over “Hitler was right” item

August 26, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

TV broadcaster Ongehoord Nederland (ON!) is facing fresh calls to have its licence revoked in the wake of an online panel show that presented Nazi leader Adolf Hitler as an anti-globalist crusader.

The segment, Let’s Twist Again, featured a clip of Hitler delivering a tirade against a “rootless international clique”, prompting one person in the crowd to shout out: “Jews!”

Presenter Arlette Adriani then asked the two panellists, Joost Niemöller and Raisa Blommestijn, to comment on the statement: “The cosmopolitan elite is compelled to take an essentially hostile position towards the ordinary indigenous people”. Both said they agreed.

MPs from the coalition parties CDA and D66, as well as the left-wing opposition party Pro, tabled questions in parliament asking culture minister Rianne Letschert if ON! should be taken off the air.

The public broadcasting ombudsman Margo Smit said she had received around 20 complaints about the item since it was put online on July 31, most of them in the last week.

“This fragment is proof that this broadcaster is deliberately flouting basic standards,” Pro MP Mohammed Mohandis told RTL.

“Nazi propaganda”

Oufa Oualhadj, for D66, said: “This thinking is bound up with Nazi propaganda and the depiction of people such as Jews as the enemy by presenting them as a rootless international force that supposedly undermines national communities.”

ON!’s director-general Peter Vlemmix said Niemöller and Blommestijn had made it clear during the broadcast that they felt “nothing but disgust for Hitler’s regime and the barbaric consequences of it”.

But he admitted that the channel had “not paid enough attention to the sensitivities around this subject”. “We should have approached them more carefully in this video.”

ON! has faced repeated calls to have its licence withdrawn since it started broadcasting in 2022. It has been fined for broadcasting misleading information and was found to have used discriminatory language when it advertised the post of editor-in-chief with the words: “man or woman, no X”.

Blommestijn received a criminal conviction for discrimination for a social media post in which she used the term “negroid primates” to describe a group of black men who were filmed assaulting a white man.

“Complex” position

Last month a majority of MPs from all three coalition parties and Pro called on Letschert not to renew the broadcaster’s licence next year.

Erik van der Maas, of right-wing liberal party VVD, said: “There is no place in the public network for a broadcaster that is funded by taxpayers’ money but systematically breaks the rules and is not prepared to keep to them.”

But the minister said the legal position was “complex” because the public broadcasting service NPO had not asked her to withdraw ON!’s licence. “That does not take away the concerns about Omroep Nederland,” she said.

The channel’s future is due to form part of a debate in parliament on September 24.
